newsitem.title: EGYPT: Archaeologists find traces of ancient Alexandria.
newsitem.headline: Archaeologists find traces of ancient Alexandria.

text.p: Marine archaeologists have rediscovered and mapped the outlines of the sunken royal quarter of ancient Alexandria, scene of the drama between Cleopatra, Mark Antony and the Caesars.

Franck Goddio, president of the European Institute of Marine Archaeology in Paris, told a news conference on Sunday that findings by his team of 16 divers overthrew old theories based on classical descriptions of the city.

"The exact topography of the vanished royal city can be identified for the first time...from now on, the accurate maps resulting from this mission will form the basis for all future archaeological work in this zone," the institute said in a statement.

Alexandria was built for the Macedonian warrior Alexander the Great from the late 4th century BC. The Ptolemies, a dynasty founded by one of his generals, ruled Egypt from the city until the Roman invasion and it remained the capital of the country until the Arab conquest in the 7th century AD.
"Mr Goddio has answered many questions for us but he has raised many new ones too," Aziza Said, professor of classical archaeology at Alexandria University, told the news conference.

Goddio said his mainly French divers had made 3,500 dives over a period of four months, pinpointing quays, pavements, fallen columns, and ancient statues with the use of a satellite-based global positioning system (GPS).

They located what is probably the long lost island of Antirrhodos, described by the Greek geographer Strabo as the site of the royal palace, and cast new light on possible sites for Timonium, where Mark Antony committed suicide in 30 BC.
Antony wooed Cleopatra, the last pharaoh of an independent Egypt and also the mistress of Julius Caesar, in Alexandria.
The royal quarter, as expected from ancient accounts, lies on the eastern side of Alexandria's eastern harbour, within sight of the centre of the modern city.
But the only vestiges of it have been lying five to six metres (17 to 20 feet) underwater since a big earthquake and tidal wave changed the coastline in AD 335.

Goddio's team mapped an area about 1 km by 1 km (miles) using the GPS device underwater to fix to within thirty cm (one foot) the position of more than 1,000 artefacts and architectural features including sphinxes, columns, capitals, lintels and blocks inscribed with hieroglyphs.
They found especially heavy concentrations on the island and along the old sea front, encouraging archaeologists at the news conference to speculate that these were the sites of palaces.
Goddio said the artefacts on the island certainly fitted the ancient descriptions of luxury.
"What we are finding is not many limestone blocks but blocks of calcite, blocks of basalt, blocks of marble, red granite - superb construction material of great value," he said.
"But these remains can be characterised only after years of excavation work," he said.
"This is the first step in a very, very long project. We've done the base and we hope to keep working for a long time to come," he added.
